adamant.e: From Middle English adamant, adamaunt, from Latin adamantem, accusative singular form of adamās (“hard as steel”), from Ancient Greek ἀδάμαντ- (adámant-, “invincible”), oblique stem of ἀδάμας (adámas).

add.e: From Middle English adden, from Latin addō (“add, give unto”).
add.g: To join or unite (e.g. one thing to another, or as several particulars) so as to increase the number, augment the quantity, or enlarge the m

adder.e: From Middle English nadder, addere, rebracketing of “a naddere” as “an addere”, from Old English nǣdre (“snake”), from Proto-West Germanic *nadrā, from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ, from pre-Germanic *néh₁treh₂, variant of Proto-Indo-European *n̥h₁trih₂, from *(s)neh₁- (“to spin, twist”).

addict.e: Borrowed from Latin addictus, past participle of addīcō (“deliver; devote; surrender”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + dīcō (“say; declare”)
addict.g: A person who is addicted, especially to a harmful drug.

addition.e: Sense of “what is added” dates from 14th century, from Middle English addicioun, addition, from Old French adition, from Latin additiōnem, accusative singular of additiō, from addō (“add, put”).

additional.e: Borrowed from Latin additionalis. By surface analysis, addition + -al.

address.e: From Middle English adressen (“to raise erect, adorn”), from Old French adrecier (“to straighten, address”) (modern French adresser), from Proto-Romance *addīrēctiāre, from ad- (“to; towards”) + *dīrēctiāre (“to guide; to direct”), from Latin dīrēctus (“straight; right”), from dīrigō (“to lay straight; to direct”), itself from regō (“to govern, to rule”).

adhere.e: From Middle English *adheren (suggested by Middle English adherande (“adhering, adherent”, present participle)), from Latin adhaerēre, adhaesum: ad (“to”) + haerēre (“to stick”).
adhere.g: To stick fast or cleave, as a glutinous substance does; to become joined or united.

adjacent.e: Borrowed from Latin adiacēns, adiacentis, derivative of adiaceō (“to lie beside”); from ad (“to”) + iaceō (“to lie down”).
adjacent.g: Lying next to, close, or contiguous; neighboring; bordering on.

adjoining.e: From Middle English ajoinen, from Old French ajoindre, (compare French adjoindre), from Latin adiungō (“join to”), formed from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + iungō (“join”).
adjoining.g: Being in contact at some point or line; joining to.

adjourn.e: From Middle English ajournen, from Old French ajorner (French ajourner), from the phrase a jor (nomé) ("to an (appointed) day").

adjure.e: From Late Middle English adjuren (“to bind (oneself or someone) by oath to do something; to entreat or implore (someone); to question (someone) under oath”), from Anglo-Norman adjurer, Middle French adjurer, and Old French ajurer (“to bind (oneself or someone) under oath.
adjure.g: To formally command or request (someone) to do something, either in the name of a deity, or to suffer a curse or punishment if they do not c

administer.e: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.

administration.e: From Middle English administracioun, from Old French administration, from Latin administratio, from administrare; see administer; compare French administration. Equivalent to administrate + -ion.
administration.g: The act of administering; government of public affairs; the service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs; the conducting of an

administrator.e: Borrowed from Latin administrātor (literally “he that is near to attend”).
administrator.g: One who administers affairs; one who directs, manages, executes, or dispenses, whether in civil, judicial, political, or ecclesiastical affa

admirable.e: From Middle English admyrable, partly from Middle French admirable and partly from its etymon, Latin admirābilis. By surface analysis, admire + -able.
admirable.g: Deserving of the highest esteem or admiration; estimable.

admiration.e: From Middle English admiracion, borrowed from Middle French admiration, or directly from Latin admīrātiō, from prefix ad- (“to, towards”) + mīrō (“to look at”) + -ātiō.
admiration.g: A positive emotion combining wonder and approbation; the regarding of another as being wonderful; a feeling of respect for another's skills

admire.e: From Middle English admyren, borrowed from Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror, from ad + mīror (“wonder at”).
admire.g: To be amazed at; to view with surprise; to marvel at.

admissible.e: Borrowed from Middle French admissible. Equivalent to admit + -ible.
admissible.g: Capable or deserving to be admitted, accepted or allowed; allowable, permissible, acceptable.

admit.e: From Middle English admitten, amitten, borrowed from Old French admettre, amettre (“to admit”), from Latin admittō (“to allow entrance, inlet”, literally “to send to”), from ad- + mittere (“to send”).
admit.g: To allow to enter; to grant entrance (to), whether into a place, into the mind, or into consideration.

admonish.e: From Middle English a(d)monisshen, from Old French *amonir + -ishen (“-ish”), from Latin admoneō (“to remind, warn”), with regular shift of conjugation, itself from ad- + moneō (“to warn, advise”).
admonish.g: To inform or notify of a fault; to rebuke in a serious tone; to tell off.

admonition.e: From Middle English amonicioun, from Old French amonicion, from Latin admonitio, stem of admonere. The -d- was restored in English in the 17th century.
admonition.g: A rebuke by an authority that one has erred and should not persist in one's actions.

ado.e: From Northern Middle English at do (“to do”), infinitive of do, don (“to do”), see do. Influenced by an Old Norse practice of marking the infinitive by using the preposition at, att (compare Danish at gå (“to go”)).

adopt.e: From Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō; ad + optō (“to choose, desire”), equivalent to ad- + opt.
adopt.g: To take (a child, heir, friend, citizen, etc.) by choice into a relationship.

adoption.e: Borrowed from French adoption, from Latin adoptio, allied to adoptare (“to adopt”). Equivalent to adopt + -ion.

adore.e: From Middle English *adoren, aouren, from Old French adorer, aorer, from Latin adōrō (“to pray to”), from ad (“to”) + ōrō (“to speak”).

adorn.e: From Middle English adornen, adournen, from Latin adōrnāre; from ad- + ōrnō (“furnish, embellish”). Replaced earlier Middle English aournen (“to adorn”) borrowed from Old French aorner, from the same Latin source.
adorn.g: To make more beautiful and attractive; to decorate.

adrift.e: The adverb is derived from a- (prefix meaning ‘at; in; on’ showing conditions, manners, or states) + drift (noun), probably modelled after afloat.
adrift.g: In or into a drifting condition; moved (especially on water by waves and wind) without being propelled or steered.

adulteress.e: From adulter (noun) + -ess. In later use typically apprehended as the female equivalent corresponding to adulterer instead.
adulteress.g: A female adulterer, a married woman or wife who commits adultery.

adultery.e: With change of suffix, from the Old French adultere (“violation of conjugal faith”) (in Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermons, 12c.), a learnèd borrowing from Latin adulterium, from adulterō. Replaced the older form avoutrie, from the inherited Old French forms avouterie or aoulterie, while keeping its suffix. Not related to adult.
adultery.g: Sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse. See more synonyms at Thesaurus:cuckoldry

advance.e: From Middle English avauncen, avancen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman avauncier, from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre, from Late Latin ab ante, from Latin ab + ante (“before”). ⟨d⟩ added in analogy to Latin ad- (cf. Middle French advancer).

advantage.e: From Middle English avantage, avauntage, from Old French avantage, from avant (“before”), from Late Latin ab ante. The spelling with d originates in a latinizing hypercorrection, the a- being falsely supposed to be from Latin ad (see advance). For sense development, compare foredeal.
advantage.g: Any condition, circumstance, opportunity or means, particularly favorable or chance to success, or to any desired end.

adventure.e: From Middle English aventure, aunter, anter, from Old French aventure, from Vulgar Latin *adventūra, from Latin adventūrus (“about to arrive, (Vulgar Latin) about to happen”), future active participle of adveniō (“to arrive”), which in the Romance languages took the sense of "to happen, befall" (see also advene). By surface analysis, advent + -ure.
adventure.g: A feeling of desire for new and exciting things.

adventure.e: From Middle English aventuren, auntren, from Old French aventurer, from aventure.

adversary.e: From Middle English adversarie, from Anglo-Norman aversaire (in Wace's Life of Saint Margaret) and Old French aversier, aversaire (French adversaire), from Latin adversārius, from adversus (“turned toward”). By surface analysis, adverse + -ary.
adversary.g: A person, group, or thing that opposes or attacks another person or group; an opponent or rival.

adversity.e: From Old French adversité, from Latin adversitātem, the accusative singular of adversitās, from adversus, the perfect passive participle of advertō (“to turn toward”).
adversity.g: The state of adverse conditions; state of misfortune or calamity.

advertise.e: From Middle English advertisen, from Anglo-Norman advertir (“to inform”), avertir, Middle French advertir, avertir (“to warn, give notice to”), with the French -iss- infix assimilated to -ise, -ize and probably influenced by the noun advertisement.
advertise.g: To give (especially public) notice of (something); to announce publicly.

advice.e: From Middle English avys, from Old French avis, rebracketed from the phrase ce m'est a vis (“I think”, “it seems to me”, literally “it is to my view”), where vis is from Latin vīsus (“vision, sight”). The unhistoric -d- was introduced during the 15th century due to influence from advise and ad-, see advance.
advice.g: An opinion offered to guide behavior in an effort to be helpful.

advise.e: From Middle English avisen (“to perceive, consider, inform”), from Old French aviser, from avis, or from Late Latin advisō, from ad + visō.
advise.g: To give advice to; to offer an opinion to, as worthy or expedient to be followed.

advisement.e: From Middle English advisement, avisement, from Old French advisement, avisement, from adviser, aviser + -ment.

advocate.e: From Middle English advocat, advoket, from Old French advocat, from Latin advocātus (“an advocate”), from the substantivization of the perfect passive participle of advocāre (“to call for”) (see -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from a calque of Ancient Greek παράκλητος (paráklētos) (whence English paraclete).
advocate.g: Someone whose job is to speak for someone's case in a court of law; a counsel.
